judgments.title: Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad v Ang Eng Hooi & ors
judgments.catchwords: (1) in a unilateral and written undertaking given by one party, X (X’s Unilateral Undertaking), to another party (Y) with regard to a debt settlement agreement between Y and Z (Settlement Agreement) - (a) is X’s Unilateral Undertaking valid or void? In this regard, whether the Contracts Act 1950 (CA) applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking. If the CA applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking, was there “consideration” for X’s Unilateral Undertaking as understood in s 2(d) CA?; and (b) if X’s Unilateral Undertaking was valid - (i) whether ss 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act 1950 (EA) bar the admissibility of extrinsic evidence to contradict, vary, add to or subtract from the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking; and (ii) how should the court construe and enforce the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking?; and (2) upon a court’s removal of a private caveat over a piece of land, whether the registered proprietor of the land (Land Owner) can claim compensation from the caveator under s 329(1) of the National Land Code (NLC) for - (a) all legal fees incurred by the Land Owner to apply to court for the removal of the private caveat; (b) the higher interest rate imposed by a lender on the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat; (c) the higher construction cost incurred by the Land Owner with regard to the Land Owner’s construction of a building on the land, purportedly as a result of the entry of the private caveat; and (d) loss of potential business suffered by the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat.

YA Dato' Dr Alwi Bin Abdul Wahab
YA Dato' Ahmad Kamal Bin Md. Shahid

judgments.title: HILLMANLEO SDN.BHD v A.RAHIS SDN.BHD & ors
judgments.catchwords: 1. This is the Plaintiffs application in Enclosure 5 for an injunction directing the 2nd Defendant to pay directly to the Plaintiff, into the client account of the Plaintiffs solicitors, the sum of RM939,690.21. The application arises in the context of the Plaintiffs substantive claim against the Defendants in this action. 2. In essence, the Plaintiffs case is that it carried out works for the benefit of the 2nd Defendant at the behest of the 1st Defendant. The 1st Defendant is the main contractor for the relevant project. The Plaintiff contends that monies payable by the 2nd Defendant to the 1st Defendant include monies attributable to the work carried out by the Plaintiff and that those monies ought therefore to be channeled directly to the Plaintiff rather than paid to the 1 Defendant. 3. The Plaintiff characterizes the application as one concerning the manner of payment rather than the determination of its substantive entitlement. Its concern is that the 1st Defendant may receive monies from the 2nd Defendant without thereafter forwarding to the Plaintiff the amount attributable to the work it claims to have carried out. 4. The 1st Defendant opposes the application. Its fundamental position is that the Plaintiffs entitlement to RM939,690.21 is itself disputed and has not been adjudicated upon. The 1st Defendant further relies upon its pleaded case that the Plaintiff had agreed to accept RM333, 146.95 as full and final settlement of its claims relating to the works and expenses up to 19 December 2025. 5. The 2nd Defendant also opposes the application. Its position is that the contractual arrangements are between the 1st and 2nd Defendants and that it has no contractual obligation to pay the Plaintiff directly. It disputes the Plaintiffs asserted entitlement to payment from it.

judgments.title: EUROCHEM NORTH WEST 2 LLC v MT RUSSIA LLC & ors
judgments.catchwords: Conclusion and Orders I find that this application should not be dismissed outright for bad faith. The Defendants do have an arguable case in OS25, but that alone does not amount to a special circumstance. A stay is not needed to prevent OS25 from becoming nugatory. There is no real or substantial risk of conflicting decisions between this Court and the court hearing OS25. The balance of justice does not favour a stay, and the argument on judicial economy is circular. No special circumstances have been shown. I reach this conclusion with no satisfaction, given the length and delay of this litigation. Both parties bear responsibility for the fact that a Mareva application filed in December 2025 remains unresolved. This is not an outcome the Court can take pride in, and the parties should understand that the Court’s patience for interlocutory manoeuvring is limited. Turning to the Plaintiff’s alternative prayer: counsel for the Plaintiff asks that if a stay were granted, it be conditional upon undertakings as to assets. As I am not granting a stay, the issue does not arise. A conditional stay is still a stay. I add a final observation, which is not intended to express any view on the merits of Enclosure 1. A Mareva injunction is a preservative remedy. It is not intended to obstruct a defendant's ordinary business, to give the plaintiff priority over other creditors, or to punish a defendant for an alleged wrong: Pharmmalaysia Bhd v Dinesh Kumar Jashbhai Nagjibha Patel & Ors (No 2) [2004] 3 MLRH 529 (also reported at [2005] 5 CLJ 50). Consistently with that principle, a defendant subject to such an order may apply to vary it so as to permit payment of bona fide business debts and commitments and of legal costs. A variation of that kind is known, after Iraqi Ministry of Defence v Arcepey Shipping Co SA (The "Angel Bell") [1981] QB 65, as an "Angel Bell" order. If a Mareva injunction is granted on Enclosure 1, the Court will fashion the order accordingly. The precise terms including any minimum sum below which the Defendants may deal freely, permission to deal with assets in the ordinary and proper course of business, and liberty to apply to vary or discharge the order upon the determination of OS 25 will be open for argument at that hearing. For completeness, I note the Ninth Arbitration Court of Appeal’s ruling of 19 August 2026, which upheld the setting aside of the Assignment Agreement of 8 October 2025. It is a significant document. Its relevance here is limited to this: it shows that the 1st and 2nd Defendants have transferred most of D1’s assets to an entity in a jurisdiction whose sanctions regime impedes payment to Russian persons. That may be relevant to the risk of dissipation and may be raised at the hearing of Enclosure 1. It is not a matter to be resolved in this application, and I express no view on it. these reasons, Enclosure 170 is dismissed with RM8,000.00 costs payable to the Plaintiff, subject to allocator.

judgments.title: WAN FAZILAWATI BT WAN HUSSIN & ors v KHABIR AKMAL BIN KAMARUDIN & ors
judgments.catchwords: PROSEDUR SIVIL – rayuan terhadap keputusan Hakim Mahkamah Sesyen – sama ada HMS terkhilaf dalam membenarkan tuntutan kecuaian perubatan – sama ada pemberian ganti rugi adalah wajar dan munasabah. KECUAIAN PERUBATAN – tuntutan terhadap kecuaian Perayu pertama yang menyuntik ubat Azitromycin secara terus (bolus) – sama ada telah melanggar kewajipan berjaga-jaga (duty of care). PROSEDUR SIVIL – sama ada Responden-Responden mempunyai kapasiti dan locus standi yang sah – Perayu-Perayu gagal mendedahkan di dalam pliding – sama ada dihalang (estopped) daripada membangkitkannya - Aturan 18 Kaedah 8(1)(a)&(b) Kaedah-Kaedah Mahkamah 2012. PROSEDUR SIVIL – sama ada Responden-Responden sebagai pihak yang berkepentingan boleh membawa tindakan jika pentadbir belum dilantik - Seksyen 7(2) Akta Undang-Undang Sivil 1956 - Seksyen 7(8) Akta Undang-Undang Sivil 1956. UNDANG-UNDANG KETERANGAN – sama ada kegagalan membuat bedah siasat menghalang Mahkamah membuat dapat mengenai punca kematian – kesan kegagalan mematuhi SOP KKM berkenaan bedah siasat ke atas pesakit di bawah umur 5 tahun - sama ada penyebab kematian (causation) boleh dibuktikan melalui inferens – sama ada keterangan menunjukkan inferens kuat si mati meninggal dunia akibat suntikan ubat Azitromycin. UNDANG-UNDANG KETERANGAN – sama ada anggapan bertentangan (adverse inference) di bawah Seksyen 114(g) Akta Keterangan terpakai – kegagalan mengemukakan laporan mortality meeting – kegagalan memanggil Doktor yang merawat si mati sejurus selepas suntikan. PROSEDUR SIVIL – prinsip dalam pemberian ganti rugi kemurungan dan depresi sebagai ibu-bapa – sama ada dihadkan sebagai kesedihan statutori (statutory bereavement) – Responden-Responden mengalami kecederaan psikiatri klinikal (psychiatric injury), kemurungan serius dan trauma psikologi yang berpanjangan – Seksyen 7(3A) Akta Undang-Undang Sivil 1956. PROSEDUR SIVIL – prinsip dalam pemberian ganti rugi kesakitan dan penderitaan (pain and suffering) – si mati mengalami kesakitan yang dahsyat, menangis dan meronta-ronta selama 15 minit sebelum tidak sedarkan diri – sama ada perlu pembuktian tempoh penderitaan yang berpanjangan. PROSEDUR SIVIL – prinsip dalam pemberiaan ganti rugi khas – pengurusan jenazah dilakukan secara mengejut – sama ada ketiadaan resit rasmi adalah material dalam hal keadaan kes ini. PROSEDUR SIVIL – prinsip dalam pemberian ganti rugi teladan dan teruk (exemplary and aggravated damages) – sama ada wajar atas salah laku dan sikap pihak hospital – keengganan mendedahkan laporan mortality meeting – cubaan meletakkan kesalahan ke atas ibu si mati – cubaan menyalahkan Responden-Responden atas kegagalan membuat post morterm – membangkitkan isu locus standi pada saat akhir – dakwaan cuba menyembunyikan punca sebenar kematian. PROSEDUR SIVIL – sama ada pemberian kadar faedah dikira dari tarikh kematian dan bukannya tarikh penghakiman adalah terkhilaf – Seksyen 11(1) Akta Undang-Undang Sivil 1956 - Aturan 42 Kaedah 12 Kaedah-Kaedah Mahkamah 2012. PROSEDUR SIVIL - rayuan ditolak - kos RM 10,000 tertaklukk kepada alokatur.
judgments.judge: YA Tuan Ariff Azami bin Hussein

judgments.title: LIM YEW CHENG v LOH PENG SEE @ PANSY LOH
judgments.catchwords: Catchwords: This is an appeal on my decision dated 15 September 2026 dismissing the Defendant’s Notice of Application dated 22 May 2026 – Enclosure 32 is an application to set aside the Ex Parte Order dated 23 February 2026 – The Leave Order by the Plaintiff - whereby the P1 was granted leave to levy execution based on a Consent Judgment dated 12 September 2012 – pursuant to Order 46 Rule 2(1)(a) Rules of Court 2012 – The judgment was entered by consent of the Defendant in favour of the Plaintiff on 12 September 2012, where it was adjudged that the Defendant should pay the Plaintiff the sum of RM483,800.00 – with interest at the rate of 4.00% per annum and costs by way of instalment payments at the due dates fixed in the Judgment commencing 15 October 2012 until 31 October 2015 – Part payments were made towards the Judgment by the Defendant and continued until 30 April 2025 – The repayments made by the Defendant were irregular in terms of timing and random in terms of the sums paid, and not in compliance with the terms of the Judgment – sometime in 2022, the Defendant agreed to defray some of the Plaintiff’s costs and expenses towards payment of the Judgment debt, in addition to making some cash payments sporadically which continued until 30 April 2025 – The particular of payments made by the Defendant, which the Plaintiff managed to ascertain from his available records at the time of Leave Application, the manner of payment, and the sums paid by the Defendant are set out – Based on the records available to the Plaintiff at the time of the Leave Application, as at 30 April 2025 the Defendant had made payment of RM139, 773.86 towards the Judgment debt – Based on the records available to the Plaintiff at the time of the Leave Application, the Judgment debt remained unsatisfied to date to the extent of RM344,026.14 with interest accruing – Defendant submitted to warrant the setting aside of the Ex Parte Order on the basis: (i) The Plaintiff’s Affidavit in Support silent on the mandatory requirement under Order 46 rule 3 of the ROC 2012 to furnish reasons for the delay in enforcement; and (ii) The Plaintiff failed to make full and frank disclosure of material facts to this Court – the Plaintiff submitted that the four conditions of legal requirement for leave have been satisfied as affirmed in its affidavit in support of the leave application – the Plaintiff has provided sufficient reasons for the delay in issuance of execution as affirmed – Order 46 rule 3 (2) ROC 2012, four (4) conditions to be satisfied: (i) identify the Judgment – rule 3(2)(a); (ii) state the amount of the original Judgment debt – rule 3(2)(a); (iii) state the amount remaining due at the date of the Leave Application – rule 3(2)(a); and (iv) provide the causes for the delay – rule 3(2)(b) – The grant of leave under Order 46 rule 2(1)(a) ROC 2012 is at the discretion of the Court – The Plaintiff had been considerate towards the Defendant by allowing the Defendant the opportunity to fulfill her repayment obligation, even beyond the instalment dates stipulated under the Judgment – the Plaintiff had even allowed the Defendant the latitude to make payment of the Plaintiff’s costs and expenses – In law, forbearance to issue execution pending settlement negotiations has been recognised as an acceptable grounds for delay by granting an extension of time for payment of a judgment debt – the Court of Appeal affirmed that part payments were a sufficient reason for delay in execution on a judgment – the negotiations and leeway between the Plaintiff and the Defendant following part payment are sufficient reasons for delay – to disallow the Plaintiff to enforce the Judgment against the Defendant would unjustly deprive the Plaintiff of its rightful recourse and also denying the Plaintiff its rights to the fruits of litigation – it is the Defendant’s own tardiness in delaying repayment of the Judgment debt. There are overwhelming evidence adduced which negates any

judgments.catchwords: CIVIL PROCEDURE: Summary judgment — Rules of Court 2012, Order 14 rule 1 — Application for summary judgment by lender under Shariah-based financing facility — Admitted reporting breaches by borrower — Certificate of Indebtedness — Triable issue — Lender’s 9-month delay in releasing first disbursement — Causation — Whether lender's funding delay caused project failure — Stay of execution — Order 14 rule 3(2) — Counterclaim arising from same factual matrix — Whether execution of summary judgment should be stayed pending trial of counterclaim. CONTRACT: Financing agreement — Shariah-based facility (Al-Musa’adah and Al-Nusrah Funds under Halal Technology Development Fund 2) — Termination — Prevention principle — Lender relying on borrower's reporting defaults to terminate — Whether lender precluded from terminating where defaults were caused or materially contributed to by lender's own 9-month delay in releasing funds. CONTRACT: Express terms — Discretion to withhold disbursement — Funding Agreement, Schedule E, Clause 1(c)(ii) — Lender withholding funds pending technical audit into non-disclosed related-party transaction — Audit clearing transaction as arm's length — Whether continued withholding of funds was a reasonable exercise of contractual power — Questions of fact to be determined at trial. CONTRACT: Entire agreement clause — Parol evidence rule — Pre-contractual oral assurances — Borrower asserting oral representation allowing retrospective expense claims up to four months — Funding Agreement containing express clauses disclaiming pre-contractual representations and entire agreement clause — Whether oral representation capable of overriding unambiguous written terms. BANKING & FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS: Islamic financing — Certificate of Indebtedness — Guarantee and Indemnity — Conclusive evidence clause — Conclusiveness of certified debt in the absence of manifest error or fraud — Shift of burden to defendant in Order 14 proceedings. EVIDENCE: Pleadings — Proof of quantum — Counterclaim for RM2,808,500.00 — Asserted loss unsupported by contemporaneous receipts or verified invoices — Pleadings are not evidence — Strict proof of quantum required at trial.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Mohd Aimi Zaini bin Mohd Azhar

judgments.catchwords: Defamation — Libel — Social media publications — Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook posts . Defamatory imputations labeling Islamic preacher as "Ustaz Scammer", "penunggang agama", "pencuri duit zakat", and "pencabul wanita" . Imputations of crime, dishonesty, financial fraud, and sexual misconduct . Statements defamatory per se . Identification of plaintiff — Extrinsic evidence and court cause list identifying plaintiff . Publication to third parties . Secondary publisher liability — Re-posting third-party video on social media — Liability of re-publisher as primary author . Presumption of publication — Evidence Act 1950, s. 114A . Defamation — Defences — Justification — Pleadings — Strict requirement to specifically plead particulars of justification . Imputation of criminal offence requiring proof of underlying truth of the criminal act, not mere police investigation or remand . Defendants bound by pleadings — Unpleaded facts raised post-trial inadmissible . Defence of justification failed . Defamation — Defences — Fair comment — Distinction between statements of fact and comment . Defamatory imputations of fraud, theft, and sexual misconduct constituting assertions of fact . Defence defeated by malice — Retaliatory posts after Notice of Demand, failure to verify allegations, and absence of apology demonstrating malice .
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Mohd Aimi Zaini bin Mohd Azhar

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case
coram: YA Dato Rhodzariah binti Bujang
YA Dato' Nordin Bin Hassan
YA Dato' Azmi Bin Ariffin

parties.label: PLAINTIF
names: FIRST WORLD HOTELS & RESORTS SDN. BHD.

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: LAU YEE SUM (BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA PERUNDING JUTERA)
LEE YONG CHIEW (BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA YC LEE ARCHITECT)
ZAHIRUDDIN BIN ZAINAL ( BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA ZAHIRUDDIN TOWN PLANNING SERVICES)

judgments.catchwords: Tort — quia timet action by neighbouring landowners to restrain a proposed highland mixed development — claims in breach of statutory duty, private nuisance, trespass and negligence — safety and stability of shared Class III and Class IV slopes — whether excavation, piling and slope-cutting at the toe of the slopes threatened loss of natural lateral and vertical support to adjoining land, occupied hotel complex and access road — expert evidence, court-appointed expert, weight and independence of party experts — planning law — whether a valid and subsisting planning permission and development order existed under Part IV of the Town and Country Planning Act 1976 — lapse of planning permission under s 24 for failure to commence development in the specified manner within twelve months — whether demolition, site clearance, notices or subdivision constituted lawful commencement — earthworks and building plan approvals under the Street, Drainage and Building Act 1974 and the Uniform Building (Pahang) By-Laws 1996 — contravention of the Guidelines on Development Planning in Hills and Highlands and the National Physical Plan — Special Management Area exemption — private road — possession, control and regulation of access — natural right of support under s 44(1)(b) of the National Land Code — collateral challenge and second actor principle — remedies — declarations, prohibitory and mandatory injunctions, restoration of the toe of the slopes, general damages — aggravated and exemplary damages refused — counterclaim for losses, delay, idleness and reputational harm dismissed — costs on a party and party basis.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Hajah Aliza binti Sulaiman
